def: Describing servers, networks and everything else in text files, so they can be reviewed, versioned and rebuilt the same way every time.
Building infrastructure by clicking in a console. Quick once, but nothing records exactly what was done, so it can't be repeated reliably.
Saying what you want to exist, and letting the tool work out the steps. Terraform and Kubernetes both work this way.
The plugin that lets Terraform talk to one platform, such as hashicorp/aws for AWS.
One thing Terraform manages, like a bucket or a VPC, written as a resource block with a type and a name.
The command that carries out a plan: creating, changing or destroying real resources.
A change Terraform can't make in place, so it destroys the resource and creates a new one. Read these lines in a plan carefully.
The file that records exactly which provider versions a project uses, so everyone gets the same ones. Commit it to git.
A setting passed into Terraform code, like the environment name, so the same code builds different copies.
A file of values for input variables, usually one per environment, such as dev.tfvars.
A name for a value worked out once inside the code, like a standard name prefix, so it isn't repeated everywhere.
A value Terraform prints after apply and passes to other code, like a VPC's ID.
Makes one copy of a resource per item in a map or set, keyed by name, so removing one item removes only that one.
Makes a number of copies of a resource, known by position. Removing an item from the middle of a list shifts the positions and destroys the wrong things.
Settings on a resource that change how Terraform replaces or protects it, such as prevent_destroy and create_before_destroy.
A folder of Terraform code used as a building block, with its own inputs and outputs, like a function.
The folder you run terraform in. It calls child modules and holds the backend and provider settings.
A second configuration of the same provider, usually for another region, chosen per resource or per module.
Several state files for one folder of code. Useful for short-lived copies; separate folders per environment are clearer for dev and prod.
Bringing a resource that already exists into Terraform's state, so the code manages it from now on.
Tells Terraform a resource was renamed in the code, so it updates the state instead of destroying and recreating the resource.
A plan that only reads what's really in AWS and shows how the state would change, without proposing any changes to AWS.
